The Hunt for Red October
THE THRILL OF THE HUNT
The Hunt for Red October

In the Orwellian year of 1984, President Ronald Reagan's hard-line policy against the Soviet Union - a nation he characterized as the 'evil empire' - helped him win a landslide reelection vote. On the Hollywood front, the Cold War fantasy Red Dawn was screening nationwide and the blockbuster Commiebashing Rambo was in the works. That same year, Maryland insurance broker Tom Clancy saw his first novel, The Hunt for Red October - an intelligent thriller about a renegade Soviet naval captain who attempts to defect with a super-sub under his command - become a phenomenal best-seller. Six years later, Paramount's $35 million film version of Clancy's book would be released in a world changed by the revolution of glasnost and perestroika. With Cold War animosities seemingly fading like a fever dream, the pundits were wondering on the eve of the film's release whether The Hunt for Red October was an irrelevancy, a relic of the old world. But the book had been praised for its intricate plotting and technical accuracy - prompting rumors that Clancy had even been debriefed by the White House. The filmmakers would not only attempt to capture the technical and emotional dynamics of the mysterious world of nuclear submarines, but mine the premise for mythic riches. "To condense the four-hundred-page novel into a screenplay," said director John McTiernan, "we had to find the key to the story. The Hunt for Red October is a sea story, and all sea stories are the same: a boy goes down to the sea in ships, is swept off into a weird world filled with colorful male characters, learns how to be a man and comes home forever changed. It's the story of Jack Ryan - a young CIA bureaucrat - and it's about his transformation." McTiernan - who had sent Arnold Schwarzenegger into the jungle for a mano a mano with a warrior from outer space in Predator and locked Bruce Willis in a high-tech skyscraper to battle a brutal criminal band in Die Hard - also saw the chance to film a different kind of action-thriller. "There are a lot of movies that portray military people as all crazy or gung-ho. The people in The Hunt for Red Octoberare thoughtful, well-educated, professional. That's why I liked doing the film. It's an adventure - a conflict that happens in men's minds. Consequently, it's much more difficult to portray." The making of the film would also be an adventure, beginning with the preproduction opportunity for key members of the crew and cast to embark on a nuclear-powered voyage to the bottom of the sea. "One of the conditions of Paramount was that I had to have Navy cooperation in making the film," said producer Mace Neufeld, who had optioned the movie rights after reading galleys of the book in 1983. "I went to the Pentagon to meet with the Secretary of the Navy. I soon learned that Tom Clancy has fans in some very high places - including a roomful of admirals. I told them that we wanted to be accurate within the bounds of classified material. So the Navy said, 'We're taking you for a submarine ride.' I spent five days underwater in the North Atlantic on the nuclear submarine Rickover. It was an invaluable experience that enabled me - plus some others from our production - to get a real sense of how submarines operate. When a sub captain goes out with his sub, he's assigned a very large geographic area. He's like the lone gunfighter. Nuclear submarines are constantly moving and are very difficult to detect. The sub's nuclear power plant allows it to stay submerged for months at a time without the need to refuel. On the sub, there are no portholes - basically you are blind except for sonar. The power plant takes up about the rear two-thirds of the ship, with the crew living and working in the front." It was obvious that capturing the tremendous scale of the modern nuclear sub would be a major production challenge. "Nuclear submarines are really cities underwater," marveled McTiernan. "It was a primary task to try to recreate that." But McTiernan - whose films have featured heroes fighting through seemingly insurmountable crisis situations - was not so entranced by the hardware that he lost sight of the human element. "The nuclear submarines are most amazing in their social and management engineering. You put a hundred men in a craft, seal it up and send it out for months. It's one thing to invent the hardware; it's another to get people to survive it. The Navy has spent years learning how - they have basically invented the space station. It's an amazing human accomplishment." The human factor would also provide the crisis conflict of the film. The Hunt for Red October commences with Captain Marko Ramius (Sean Connery) guiding the Red October - the latest in Soviet submarine technology - out of its port base in Murmansk on a maiden voyage to test its operational capabilities. Once underway and underwater, Ramius cooly murders the vessel's political officer and sets into motion a daring plan to defect to the West with his billion-dollar trophy. As described in the novel and depicted on screen, the Red October is a modified Typhoon class ballistic missile submarine essentially equal in size to a World War Il aircraft carrier. Sixhundred-and-fifty feet in length, the thirty-thousand-ton vessel carries twenty-six SS-N-20 Seahawk missiles - each with eight five-hundred-kiloton independently targetable nuclear warheads. The sub also has a deadly technological twist - a new caterpillar drive system that enables it to move undetected through the ocean. Chasing the silent giant through the watery vastness are two attack submarines about half its size - the Los Angeles class USS Dallas and the Soviet Alfa class Konovalov. "The initial thought after getting the Navy's cooperation was that we would do the filming on real subs - which proved impossible," Neufeld recalled. "It was too difficult to get equipment and lighting into a sub. Next we thought we could build the subs and outfit them with equipment from naval suppliers. But real sub equipment proved too heavy because everything on a sub is anchored down - a drafting table on the Rickover weighed a thousand pounds! Then we were doing some shooting at a Navy submarine simulator and we decided to build, in effect, our own simulator that could tilt and roll to duplicate the sensation of a sub diving and banking." Meetings between Di Sarro, McTiernan, Marsh and second unit director Beau Marks helped focus the design. Once the specifications were complete, Di Sarro and engineer Robert Graham began work on the gimbals. "The design called for two separate forty-by-forty-foot platforms seventeen feet off the ground." said Di Sarro. "Each gimbal had to hold thirty to forty thousand pounds of set plus seventy to eighty cast and crew. Each completed gimbal weighed sixteen tons." Massive hydraulic mechanisms were needed to effect precise tilt and roll requirements. Di Sarro likened the basic system to the U-joint of an automobile which gives the axle its motion flexibility. But while an automobile U-joint is all of four inches long, the hydraulic rams needed to actuate the gimbal were four feet long and a foot thick. "The hydraulic rams attached to the platforms were connected to a hydraulic valve," said Di Sarro, "and from there to an electronic joystick. The one hydraulic power unit provided power for the two gimbals, each of which was on a different set." The gimballed sets also required complex wiring and electronics. Since space within the claustrophobic interiors was at a premium, pains were taken to wire the lighting directly into the settings. Rick Thompson - Di Sarro's electronic foreman - also wired power to the requisite gauges, lights, graphs, readouts and control panels. Since little or no illumination penetrates into the ocean levels frequented by submarines - and since the submarines themselves have no external lighting - a degree of stylization was required in order for anything at all to be seen on film. It was McTiernan's notion to create a flow of phosphorescent microorganisms and particulate matter around the boats - a phenomenon which actually occurs to some degree - and keep the submarines dark against a dark background with changing tonalities. Modelmaker Greg Jein was hired by Boss as an independent contractor to fabricate the subs - a massive task which consumed nearly five months. The submarine designs reflected the search for accuracy - and the need for accommodating national security concerns. "I met with John McTiernan and he described to me what he wanted with the subs," said Jein. "In addition, I have a collection of sub photos that I worked from. We also had David D. After nearly a year of model construction and effects preproduction, Boss Film submitted a series of film tests to the producers and the studio. Though the look they had captured conformed to the criteria established by the director, the results on screen met with less than enthusiastic response. After several further attempts to reconcile artistic vision with nuts-and-bolts technology - a process which strained relations between the director and the effects facility - it was decided that a radically different approach was needed and that the job should be pulled from Boss and sent elsewhere. It was not an unprecedented move given the mercurial dynamics of big-budget filmmaking, but it was one that would create a tight shooting schedule for the next effects house. When Industrial Light and Magic was given the assignment in mid-October - along with all models, stock footage, move tests and storyboards produced at Boss - the company had slightly more than three months to design and complete some fifty effects shots so that the film could meet its March 1990 opening. Effects producer Kimberly Nelson was responsible for assembling the ILM team and overseeing the concentrated effects effort. "It was a challenge - we had three months to accomplish what usually takes a year. We were also shooting very late in the postproduction schedule. Since we had a short amount of time, we wanted to play the production safe and not sorry. So people were assembled who worked well together and could think on their feet." In addition to the deadline pressures, the quickly assembled crew had to realize a visual effects vision unique in the annals of submarine movies. "There was a big difference between this film and the old submarine movies," observed effects director of photography Patrick Sweeney. "Those old films were pretty static and murky - you couldn't see much. John McTiernan wanted The Hunt for Red October played more dramatically - with subs chasing each other, firing torpedoes, almost ramming each other." Several options were considered for depicting the submarines. The possibility of digitally processing submarine imagery was briefly considered, but could not be pursued given the strict deadline. It was finally decided that the submarine models would be filmed using motion control, but in-camera against miniature environments rather than with bluescreen. The underwater environment would be conjured up, literally, out of smoke. "The whole idea was to keep the opticals to a minimum and let the ships work within a smoke environment," said effects supervisor Scott Squires. "We had tested in water, but smoke seemed the most practical for simulating the depth and texture you would get underwater - especially given the time frame. For the smoke, we used cracker oil smoke which does not shift or move around. We would run an air hose down a pipe into a metal drum that stood three feet high and a foot-and-a-half wide. At the bottom was a ring with little holes - like an oldfashioned sprinkler head - where the smoke could escape. Air would blow through the tube and break up the oil, creating droplets. To handle the Red October assignment, an expansive stage area was required not only to accommodate motion control tracks, cameras, rigs, lights, fax machines, video and other equipment, but also to provide a large area for the submarine models to work in scale with one another during multiple sub shots. In an industrial area in nearby Richmond, a suitable structure was found and secured - an empty warehouse used for fruit storage in the summer months. The effects crew dubbed the facility 'Fruit Bay' and began converting it to their needs. During the setup phase, the ILM model shop took inventory of the existing submarine models. There were two Red October models - twenty-one and four feet long - a nine-foot Konovalou sub, two ten-foot Dallas attack subs and a two-foot rescue submersible. "Once they arrived," said Squires, "the models were all motorized with rotatable propellers, sliding hull doors and other moving parts. We built a mid-size eleven-foot Red October - also a second bottom of the large-scale Red October because two or three new shots the director wanted featured just the bottom of the ship. The model people had to match it with the original so there would be no conflicts." Fully configured, the Fruit Bay facility would be divided into two stage areas. The largest - which would accommodate the bulk of the shooting - had fifteen thousand square feet of floor space and was twenty-nine feet from floor to rafters. "When we first came to the warehouse," said Sweeney, "we looked at the ceiling and said, 'Boy, if it were twice as big it would be twice as good. Typically we began each shot with the motion control camera as close to the subs as we could get. But if the sub tracked away thirty-five to forty feet, we were suddenly fighting the ceiling and floor creeping into the top and bottom of the frame - even with the widescreen 2:3.5 shooting format. I always had to frame out the light sources at the top of the frame, but we could neutralize the brightness on the floor with different colored pieces of canvas that matched our color scheme for the particular shot we were doing." All the cables ran through a multicable back to a dimmer board and control console that had a hundred-and-seventy-two individual slide dimmers. The setup gave us maximum control of more than two hundred individual lights." The dimmers were vital for maintaining the haze effect desired for the underwater shots. "One problem we had was that a model might be traveling thirty to forty feet for a shot," Fitzsimmons explained, "but if we lit it all at once, the flash in the exposure would be too bright and we would not have any definition in the background ships. All of the lights were hooked up to a large theatrical-type dimming board. That way, if the camera was doing a ninety-degree pan, we could also dim our background curtain of light. The job of R. A. Johnson - our dimmer operator - was to bring the lights up as the sub went through an area. We tried to estimate the timing for the dimming - a lot was done to my eye. Then R. A. had to sit at the control board like a Zen master and work the control slide so the lights would not appear to just pop on during the motion control movement. Many of our light cues required dimming from fifty percent to one hundred percent in five to fifteen minutes. At these slow camera speeds it was important to do the cues very slowly." Various rigs and mounts were required to place the models in their simulated underwater world. "Typically," said Squires, "we placed the twenty-one-foot Red October on a pylon mount hidden out of frame with the sub motorized to roll and move on the track while it was mounted. Rigging the models and cameras for each shot required careful preparation. Part of the difficulty of the setup was that in many shots we had to see two or three subs at the same time - all of them in scale to each other. We also had to see the second sub in the background and get a sense of how the ships maneuvered against each other." To get the height and reach necessary for the main rig, a twelve-foot-high bank of scaffolding was used. "The scaffolding was anchored down and supported for stability," said Sweeney. "We then put a fifty-foot-long motion control track on top of the scaffold to give us fifty feet of run for the models. Next we took a Chapman crane arm off its base and put it on a motion control base." Adapting it for motion control use was a major short-notice project. "Normally it takes six months to make a motion control crane," said stage technician Joe Fulmer. "We had to do this one in two days. You have to be cautious with a crane. You motorize a big thing like that where you have a couple tons of weight moving up and down a track and it can get away from you if you don't mind it." The flying wire rig that would attach to the motion control track was a pivotal piece of production business. With the crane arm moving in a linear direction twenty-five feet or more along the track, the wire rig had to be constructed both to provide a separate motion control mechanism for the required pitch and roll simulation and to keep the model in perfect balance. If a sub suspended from the wire rig were to wobble, it would destroy the illusion of a giant ship moving with a powerful underwater motion. Called in to consult on the rigging apparatus was Tad Krzanowski, who had developed similar, though lighterweight systems to fly the spacecraft models in Batteries Not Included and the submersibles for The Abyss. "For Batteries," said Krzanowski, "the director wanted a smooth gentle motion for the spaceships. But the models were round and weighed only ten pounds. The ships in The Abyss were also fairly lightweight. The submarine models in Red October, however, were long tubes - forty to forty-five pounds on average - with a lot of gravity pulling at them and they had to be rigged for the turn, tilt and banking motions of a real submarine. It was very difficult to establish the hanging points to keep the subs balanced because they were also heavy in the back. The Batteries rig had three hanging points, but we needed four hanging points for the subs - with each point requiring three wires in a triangulate pattern to keep the suspended models balanced." Although the flying wire rig was strong enough to support even the two-hundredand-fifty-pound Red October - as it did on several occasions - unnecessary stress on the wires was avoided by removing stepper motors and other extraneous internal mechanisms before wiring the model. "The design went through several stages," Krzanowski said. "At the end of the crane arm was a motion control rotator that was the tilt and roll mechanism for each model. Next was a gimbal which transferred the motion of the motion control rotator to the submarine. The gimbal was much like a helicopter swash blade which is the mechanism between the helicopter's stationary and moving mechanism that provides flexibility for pitch, roll and tilt motions. The gimbal is like the master mover, with the sub following through the wire linkage and the whole apparatus moving by motion control. Between the gimbal swash blade and the model was a four-foot-square aluminum frame that we called the 'star. The star was a unit that spread the wires apart to provide stability for the suspended model. To achieve that, we would drop our wires from the four corners of the frame to each of the support points - three wires at each point forming a triangle." It was vital that all twelve wires be rigged under tension in the perfect triangulate pattern. If even one wire was out of the place, the model would wobble. "The wires spread down from the star, attaching to the sub at two hanging points in front and two in the back. "We would arrive in the morning and start setting up and rigging the models," Sweeney explained. "I would design the lights and program the motion control until early afternoon. During the course of the day, we would be in communication with John. The hard part was setting up the shot, programming the motion control and lighting it. The shooting was easy. Around 8 p.m., we would be able to start the smoke and shoot the scene. With the motion control camera shooting a frame per second, it usually took fifteen minutes to half-an-hour to get one shot." "There were easy shots and difficult shots," Squires observed. "One of the most difficult was one that cameraman Marty Rosenberg did. We had the large Red October mounted on a pylon and Marty had to go over the deck of the ship. The camera had to be mounted - suspended - and we had to rig it all out so we could literally fly right across the deck and over to the other side, scraping the sub all the time. That took a lot of setup to accomplish." Most of the shots employed Vistavision cameras and wide-angle lenses. "Vistavision cameras are bulky - which prevents getting any closer than several inches to the model. With the submarine models, those several inches translated to about twenty-five feet above the deck - not enough to provide the sense of scale and mass required. To get in close, we had a few mirrors made up for the lenses. The mirrors were arranged the same as on a snorkel lens - above or below the lens at a forty-five-degree angle. Pacific Title absorbed some more of the overflow by pulling bluescreen elements for The Optical House. In Hoboken, the rock-bursting shot had to be redone because it was decided that the high-speed frame rate was wrong. Also redone was the exterior bay shot of the shuttlecraft crashing in. Everyone was thoroughly exhausted. Some of the sacrifices made in the final cut were disheartening to Peter Wallach and his people. Orphaned was the Pioneer probe explosion, leaving behind a spectacular reel of outtakes. A streaked element for the warp drive effect that resembled neon was not used because it deviated from the imagery established in previous Star Trek films. In the exterior bay entry, the shuttlecraft's thrusters flying off in a mass of flame were excised as an editorial option. But within the context of the enormous time constraint, the entire effects operation was truly a ninetyday wonder. Star Trek V did not receive many thumbs up in the media - or at the boxoffice. Devoted audiences noted the inherent weaknesses of the storyline and may have been chagrined by the overall lack of spectacle they had come to expect. Bran Ferren reflects on the experience with a mixture of pride and anguish. "There were many effects I would have liked to have done more imaginatively, but we were in a panic mode just trying to get everything done. We were previewing the film three weeks after the director had his cut. We were cutting negative before we even previewed. If we had not done that, we would not have made the deadline. That kind of schedule is a nightmare. If there had been six months of post, Paramount could have previewed it, decided there were fundamental issues that needed to be corrected and perhaps made a better movie. Given our time squeeze and budget restrictions, the final effect of the project could have been much worse. Overall, I was happy with what we created. ILM gets a project and they do it because they're up and running. They're all wearing the same T-shirt and the politics are confined to one facility. But if you have nothing but an empty warehouse and a three-month deadline, you have to reinvent the wheel. The best experience of all was that we started with an abandoned licorice factory, hired the best talent in the tri-state area and produced some very satisfying footage. Bran Ferren filled it with hardware and operational support. Nilo Rodis filled it with hope." Everyone shared the pain.
